description_full: Puma Biotechnology, Inc., a biopharmaceutical company, focuses on the development and commercialization of products to enhance cancer care in the United States and internationally. It offers NERLYNX, an oral version of neratinib that is used to treat adult patients with early stage HER2-overexpressed/amplified breast cancer; and advanced or metastatic HER2-positive breast cancer when combined with capecitabine. The company also develops alisertib, a small molecule inhibitor of aurora kinase A for the treatment of hormone receptor positive breast cancer, triple negative breast cancer, small cell lung cancer, and head and neck cancer. It sells its products through specialty pharmacy and distributor networks. The company has license agreements with Pfizer Inc. for the development, manufacture, and commercialization of neratinib (oral), neratinib (intravenous), PB357, and related compounds, as well as sub-license agreements with Specialised Therapeutics Asia Pte Ltd., Medison Pharma Ltd., Pint Pharma International SA, Knight Therapeutics, Inc., Pierre Fabre Medicament SAS, and Bixink Therapeutics Co., Ltd. Puma Biotechnology, Inc. was founded in 2010 and is headquartered in Los Angeles, California.

financial_summary: Puma Biotechnology Inc is a small-cap healthcare business with a $402M market cap on $228M of annual revenue.

The top line has compounded at +0% over the past three years, which puts it in mature, slow-growth territory. Operating margins are expanding by +134.1pp year-over-year, which is one of the strongest signals that the moat is deepening.
Returns on capital run at 35% against a 10% cost of capital — a 25-point spread that is the clearest signature of an economic moat.

The business throws off $42M in free cash flow — roughly 18 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 1.34× so those profits are backed by real cash.
On the balance sheet, the balance sheet carries net cash, which is the gold standard: the business never has to make desperate decisions in a bad year, and interest coverage runs at 5.6×.

Shareholder yield is only 0.0%, a thin return of capital, and insiders hold 15% of the shares, so management thinks like owners because it is one — the strongest alignment there is, and within its sector the business captures 1.9× its fair share of profits, a structural advantage visible in the numbers.
